subjects.introduction: The Kurds remembered a voice lifted in prayer every night on the mountain; they could not make out the words, only that someone was pleading with God. For two years Bahá’u’lláh lived in that solitude at Sar-Galú, calling Himself Darvísh Muḥammad, having left wealth and home so that, as He later wrote, the fire of hatred might die down. The cost fell on others too: in Baghdad the Cause went silent, and two young believers who knocked at ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s door sat on the floor and wept for an hour when told that no one knew where He was. Yet solitude never quite held. Learned men of Sulaymáníyyih sought Him out, an illiterate shepherd left his flock each day to hear Him speak, and at last a traceless One was found in a cave by friends bearing petitions. Mark’s picture of Jesus praying alone and then going on to the next towns offers a smaller pattern of withdrawal and return [1]. The return itself opened a door that never closed again, and the story continues into Bahá’u’lláh’s early ministry, His life in Baghdad, and the banishments that followed.
subjects.arc: Begin with the remembered sound of prayer, enter the solitude and its cost, then follow encounters, the search, and the return to community.

order.why: Open with the remembered voice of prayer and the simplicity of the returning figure.
Enter the account of a remote mountain refuge.
Hear the withdrawal described in Bahá’u’lláh’s own words.
shortened: Upon My arrival in Iraq, detached from all else save God, I withdrew for two years. Singly and alone I departed for the wilderness and severed Myself from the world and its peoples. But during that period of withdrawal solitude was not granted to me. Those joyous days soon passed and came to an end, and it hath not been My portion ever since.

order.why: Hold solitude beside the grief of a community without news.
shortened: For the Well-Beloved was then in Kurdistan, living in a cave at Sar-Galu; and there, entirely alone in that wasteland, with no companion, no friend, no listening soul, He was communing with the beauty that dwelt in His own heart. All news of Him was completely cut off; Iraq was eclipsed, and in mourning.

order.why: Consider fellowship with the poor as another aspect of the period.
shortened: While Baha'u'llah was in Baghdad, still in possession of great wealth, He left all He had and went alone from the city, living two years among the poor. They were His comrades. He ate with them, slept with them and gloried in being one of them.

order.why: Reflect on the title Darvish and the accompanying poetic lines.
Notice the simplicity of daily sustenance in the reported recollection.
Place the retreat within the rhythm of Ramadan.
Read the broader account of the withdrawal, writings, and learned encounters.
shortened: Perceiving the covert rebellion of Mirza Yahya and others, Baha'u'llah journeyed alone to Sulaymaniyyih and was absent for two years. During that time, Mirza Yahya was acting with utmost caution behind a veil of concealment and, fearing the attention of the General Consul of Persia in Baghdad, disguised himself, took the name of Haji 'Ali, and engaged in selling shoes and plaster in Basrah and in Suqu'sh-Shuyukh in the vicinity of Baghdad. The Cause became entirely quiescent, the Call ceased to be heard, and all name and trace thereof well-nigh vanished.

During His sojourn in Sulaymaniyyih, Baha'u'llah penned a number of works, among them certain prayers of which copies are still extant, and certain epistles on mystical wayfaring addressed to the doctors and the learned men of Islam, which are likewise still extant.

In any event, all the doctors and learned men of Sulaymaniyyih attested to the knowledge, attainments, and perfections of Baha'u'llah and developed an affection for His person; that is, they would say that this Man was unique and ranked among the chosen ones of God.

order.why: Trace how recollections of Darvish Muhammad reached Baghdad.
Follow one remembered friendship beyond the mountains.
shortened: There was a Mohamad Bey, a Kurd, of short stature, fat and a long beard. He had met Baha'u'llah when he was living in the mountain of Soleymanieh and became His ardent follower. When Baha'u'llah returned from the mountains after two years of absence, this Mohamad Bey also came to Bagdad bringing 46 mares for the governor Omar pasha.

order.why: Read the search, recognition, and entreaties for return.
shortened: Hence, Shaykh Sultan and Aqa Muhammad-Javad left for Sulaymaniyyih. There they investigated and made inquiries about His whereabouts. At last they learned that He was indeed residing on Sar-Galu mountain and that it was impossible for them to go there. So they waited in Sulaymaniyyih until He arrived. They attended His presence and presented their plea. Baha'u'llah, however, did not agree. Then they said, 'We do not want to do anything contrary to Thy blessed will but we are not leaving Thy presence either.'

order.why: Consider the reported relationship between the journey and later writings.
Complete the linked readings with the renewed promotion of the Cause amid opposition.
shortened: And when the Luminary of the horizons illumined the horizon of Iraq, no voice was raised from any direction, and no movement was observed from any body. All were found to be dead or withered while living, and were concealed behind veils from the severity of the days and the wrath of men.

When these things were witnessed, We arose to promote the Cause - an arising after which there was no sitting down. And when, through divine power, the banners of the Most Great Remembrance were raised upon the highest station of the world, the buzzing of flies emerged from behind the veil.

order.why: Begin the additional selections with the personal cost and purpose of withdrawal. Hear the search recalled through the image of a traceless figure found in a cave.
shortened: At length, abandoning My home and all that was therein, and renouncing My life and all that pertained thereunto, I retired alone and companionless. I roamed the wilderness of resignation, travelling in such wise that in My exile every eye wept sore over Me, and all created things shed tears of blood because of My anguish. The birds of the air were My companions and the beasts of the field My associates. In such wise did I, even as the flash of the spirit, pass over this fleeting world. For two years or rather less, I shunned all else but God, and closed Mine eyes to all except Him, that haply the fire of hatred may die down and the heat of jealousy abate.

At last the divine decree prompted certain spiritual souls to remember this Canaanite Youth. Armed with a number of petitions, they searched in every place and enquired from every person, until they found in a mountain cave a trace of this traceless One.

order.why: Revisit the absence of knowledge about His whereabouts.
shortened: When Baha'u'llah left Bagdad and without the knowledge of the friends went to Soleymanie, one day he saw a boy in the streets weeping.
Then all the learned and wise men of the city gather around him and after a time finding that these men have taken all his time, he retired to the mountains where nobody could reach him.

order.why: Preserve another recollection of the retreat’s settings.
shortened: Baha'u'llah departed to Sarkalu alone. Nobody knew just where he was, even we were not informed. Two years he passed at Sarkalu. Some of the time he passed in the mountains, some of the time in grottoes, and some of the time in the city of Sarkalu.

order.why: Attend to the remembered prayer beneath the moonlight.
Revisit the detail of simple food in an additional account.
Consider the two visitors whose grief conveys the community’s desolation.
shortened: These two new believers from Meelan came and knocked at the door. I went and opened it. I observed they are two young men from Meelan. Their faces were luminous, their eyes radiant. They were shining like unto two suns. I asked them to come in.

After a while they asked about the Cause. I told them the Cause is extinct, there is no Cause. They asked about Mirza Yahya, I told them he is concealed and no one knows his whereabouts. They asked about Baha'u'llah. I told them I do not know where he is.
As soon as they heard this sad news they looked at each other and began to weep and weep. For nearly one hour they sat down on the floor and wept bitter tears of regret and disappointment.

order.why: Distinguish the attraction of a living presence from borrowed religious vocabulary.
shortened: In the days of Baghdad and Sulaymaniyyih, Shaykh 'Abdu'l-Husayn was told that the Blessed Beauty was attracting the Kurds to Himself by quoting Sufi and gnostic terms. This poor Shaykh obtained a copy of the Futuhat-i-Makkiyyih [The Meccan Revelations] and committed its passages to memory. But wherever he quoted them, he saw that none lent an ear to him. He was greatly puzzled as to why people did not listen to him.

order.why: Follow the affection of a humble visitor into friendship and practical assistance.
shortened: At the time that His Holiness Baha'u'llah was in the mountains of Sulymanieh one of the young rugged, illiterate kurds inhabiting in the valleys came to see Him. The Blessed Perfection is kind to him and his love grows for Baha'u'llah. His name was Mollah Ali Mardan. Although he had the title of "Mullah" yet he was illiterate. He did not know anything about faith but ardently he adored Baha'u'llah. Everyday he would leave his flock and go to the cave to hear the Blessed Perfection speak.
Baha'u'llah received him with graciousness and open arms.

As the inspector of the custom-house was a devoted follower of the Blessed Perfection He sent for him. When he arrived, Baha'u'llah pointed Mulla Ali Mardan to him "This is my friend" He said "I hope you will give him a position in the custom House." "Very well" the inspector respectfully answered. and the "friend" of Baha'u'llah was properly installed in work with fair wages.

order.why: Read the fuller reported portrait of encounters with people of differing backgrounds.
Trace a reported clue that helped the friends locate Him.
Consider the return as described in relation to divine decree.
Close with the reopened door and the renewal of communal life.
shortened: When the Blessed Beauty returned from Sulaymaniyyih to Baghdad, He opened wide the door and gave a summons unto all. At first, one or two of the Persian adversaries came, intending to raise objections, and some said, "Once again the Babis have appeared in the light of day." But the Blessed Beauty so silenced them that thereafter all took heed of their own account.
Little by little, the blessed uprising exalted the Cause of God, rent asunder the veils, and drew souls unto the station of sanctity and detachment.

questions: What do the accounts of prayer, poverty, and friendship reveal about spiritual influence outside public recognition?
How do solitude and companionship appear together in these selections?
What becomes clearer when the movement from withdrawal to renewed engagement is compared with Mark’s account?
How do the search for Bahá’u’lláh and the grief during His absence deepen the meaning of His return?
What might the contrast between borrowed spiritual vocabulary and lived spiritual presence invite us to examine in ourselves?

neighbors.invitation: Explore generosity and detachment before the retreat.
Read another account in which separation from friends carries a deep human cost.
Consider how the experience of exile becomes a source of consolation.

references.label: 1 · Mark 1:35–39 (King James Version)
references.note: Mark describes Jesus praying in a solitary place, being sought by His companions, and proceeding to other towns to preach. Compare the relation of solitude, companionship, and mission with the Sulaymaniyyih selections. The different duration, circumstances, and religious significance of the two accounts remain important; the comparison need not turn them into a single pattern.

subjects.displayTitle: Adrianople: fellowship and proclamation in exile
subjects.introduction: Fifteen exiles in a single room, taking turns at the cooking while the Rumelian snow piled up outside, and then a spring so fine that even the chronic complainer among them praised it: this is how ‘Abdu’l-Bahá remembered the first winter in Adrianople. Beside the cheerfulness stand a lament for sick children on the road, the loneliness of a strange city, and the forced march to Gallipoli. The deepest claim about this period is Bahá’u’lláh’s own: driven to a remote place so that the lamp of guidance might be put out, He chose there to reveal His Cause in full, so that the Tablets to the kings went out from the very spot meant to silence Him. Paul, writing in chains that his imprisonment had furthered the gospel, read adversity the same way [1]. From here the journey continues into the whole sequence of Bahá’u’lláh’s banishments, into the rebellion of Mírzá Yahyá that darkened these years, and into the stories and anecdotes in which the humour of the exiles survives.
subjects.arc: Begin with communal life in a difficult winter, hear the experience of separation, then follow proclamation, renewed expulsion, and the meaning given to adversity.

order.why: Open with shared life through a severe winter and the welcome arrival of spring.
shortened: But the rest of us, who were over fifteen in number and yet were obliged to live in one single room, were nevertheless filled with joy and composure; for we were blessed with exile for the sake of the Cause of God. And in order to pass the time, each day one of us cooked a certain dish for the rest to enjoy. So the severe winter went by and in the course of a few months the snow and cold passed away and the famous delectable spring-time of Rumelia came on. Then the weather was so delightful, that even the above Haji Mirza Ahmad began to praise the glorious air of Rumelia."

order.why: Hear the loneliness and family hardships expressed in the account of the journey.
shortened: From there like captives we arrived in another city named Adrianople. Forty days of captivity had been heard of, but six months had never been heard of. Throughout this period several children were sick and ill until we found residence beyond Qaf. And now strange and alone, without companion or friend, without associate or helper, in this dark city we pass these transient days.

order.why: Read the concise account of the decree taking the exiles to Edirne.
Place this period within the wider sequence of banishments.
Notice humor within a reported encounter among companions.
Consider a recollection of the distinctive character of Bahá’u’lláh’s discourse.
Attend to the changing circumstances of meeting and association. Read the account of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s service as conditions of confinement changed.
shortened: In the Land of Mystery too, we would meet with some and grant audience to others. But in the Most Great Prison we have met with no one and have completely closed the doors of association. The Master has borne all the hardships for our comfort and ease. He has become an impregnable fortress and a mighty shield before the world and its peoples, bringing us comfort.

order.why: Read the prayer’s account of a brief withdrawal from the inhabited house.
shortened: Thou knowest, O my God, that the Dawning-Place of Revelation went forth from His inhabited house, directing His steps toward the house of His brother who was named Kalim, and there He secluded Himself for eight days and nights, which We completed with another night as a bounty from Our presence.

order.why: Hear the public invitation and willingness to await opponents. Read the additional account of the public encounter introduced earlier.
Explore the account of a fuller declaration under conditions intended to suppress it.
Connect the Adrianople period with the Tablets addressed to rulers.
Confront the abrupt removal, loss of possessions, and suffering on arrival in ‘Akká.
shortened: Nevertheless, three months ago, officials of the Ottoman state suddenly surrounded our house, seized all the belongings of my followers in the bazaar, and took them to the government building. After this, a man came from the governor and informed us that, on the orders of the Sultan, I had to go with (my wives?) and children to Gallipoli. They gave us no further notice than that. All the belongings of my followers were sold for a paltry price at the decree of the military commanders, but they did not even give us an opportunity to collect the money.

No sooner had we arrived in Acre than they imprisoned us in a ruined barracks, even the women and six-month old children, and they forthwith shut the doors of entry and exit. We have now been imprisoned in the ruined barracks for fifty days, and, on account of the badness of the water and air, we have all been stricken by serious illnesses, such that, after two days, three people died without a physician or food or medicine.

order.why: Consider the reported reasoning behind successive attempts at isolation.
shortened: Through the power of the Persian government the Blessed Perfection was then sent to Adrianople, in Roumelia, a country very far from Persian (and a possession of Turkey). Because there was no railway, there was very little travel by the Persians to and from Adrianople, and therefore, it was thought by the learned me of Persia that the Cause of god would have no effect upon the Persians. However, it was soon learned that these places were not places of banishment for the Blessed Perfection (Glory be to him!), and it was therefore decided that he should be sent to some small place--a place where murderers were confined, where robbers were imprisoned, so that this Cause would be weakened. Accordingly, the clergy, or learned men of Persia, being hostile to this holy Cause, so arranged that the Blessed Perfection was sent from Adrianople (the land of Mystery) to Acre, Syria.

order.why: Trace the interpretation of exile as an occasion of growing influence.
shortened: He was single and alone, without help or assistance and four times he was exiled. Each exile became the means of strengthening his cause. From Persia they exiled him, saying, 'Now his cause is uprooted. No more trace of him will remain.' But no! If he had not come to Baghdad his cause would not have made such progress in Persia. Then two monarchs united and exiled him from Baghdad to Constantinople. 'If he goes further fro Persia,' they said, he will be uprooted sooner.' But instead of that his cause was elevated.

order.why: Widen the view to the spread of the message beyond its original region.
shortened: And when they strove to banish and expel the manifest light from Iran, the mighty banner was raised in Iraq. And when they engaged in hypocrisy in Iraq, it caused the Ancient Beauty to be exiled to the renowned city, and the mighty drum and the greatest bell were struck in Istanbul. And when they sent Him with utmost oppression and enmity from the center of Ottoman rule to Rumelia, that region too received the rays of the manifest light. And when He was transferred from that land to the Most Great Prison, and the ruined fortress became the prison of the Beloved of the world of being, and the utmost abasement and humiliation were imposed, the call of the Cause of God and the voice of the Word of God spread to the countries of Europe and America.

order.why: Read the sequence of cities through the account’s scriptural interpretation.
Complete the linked readings with the tension between immediate grief and later benefit.
shortened: Therefore every calamity that befalls the friends of God, though outwardly it is a calamity, in reality it results in a bounty.

Similarly when they were sending Him from Constantinople to Adrianople, how much it caused sorrow to the friends to a degree that cannot be described. Likewise when from Adrianople to Akka which was the prison for criminals. When this news reached various places all the friends became distraught. This calamity affected them so much that it cannot be described, and yet this became the greatest cause of the exaltation of God's Cause. If the Blessed Beauty had not come to Akka, where would the divine power and might be manifested such that imprisonment became the cause of the proclamation of God's Cause and its fame, prison became paradise, and jail became a palace.

order.why: Close with the appeal for release from repeated, unexplained banishment.
shortened: Now, once again, we are being exiled from Adrianople without the knowledge of where we are destined and without any reason, and all our possessions were disposed of.  If the Turkish government does not welcome us any more, and as we are not of this country, let us be free to go to a country of another power.  It is to the sovereigns of Europe who like to help the oppressed that we plead, supplicating them to release us from this bondage.

questions: How do meals, humor, and acts of service change our understanding of life under exile?
How can the passages about composure and joy be read together with those expressing loneliness and anguish?
What does the comparison with Paul illuminate about finding wider meaning in an attempt at suppression?
How do the accounts distinguish spiritual influence from official power?
What responsibilities toward displaced people become clearer when attention turns from the route of exile to the experiences of families?

neighbors.invitation: Consider another period of separation and the community’s response to it.
Follow the remembrance of a companion through successive exiles.
Explore a later account of practical care for a threatened community.

references.label: 1 · Philippians 1:12–14 (King James Version)
references.note: Paul describes his confinement as an occasion for the gospel to become known and for others to speak with greater courage. Compare that interpretation with the Adrianople selections on proclamation under pressure. Their common concern with an unexpected outcome does not erase the distinct circumstances or justify the suffering inflicted on those involved.

subjects.displayTitle: Successive banishments: loss, companionship, and purpose
subjects.introduction: Four times He was rendered homeless, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes of His father: from Tihrán to Iraq, from Iraq to Constantinople, from there to Adrianople, and at last to the prison-city of ‘Akká, the most desolate fortress in the world, where the Sultan’s decree read out on the third day sentenced the exiles to perpetual confinement. The banishments of Bahá’u’lláh can be followed as a route on a map, as a chain of plunder, chains and dungeons, or through the eyes of a companion who stood before Him morning and evening in each city until he soared at last to God. They can also be read, as ‘Abdu’l-Bahá reads them, for a purpose nobody intended: every removal meant to extinguish the lamp carried its flame to new regions, until the Persian ministers themselves admitted that none of the earlier exiles had humiliated Him. Bahá’u’lláh invites a comparison with Abraham, who left country and kindred under a promise of blessing for all the families of the earth [1], though a divine summons is not the same thing as expulsion at the hands of a government, and the human cost of each departure is never hidden. The road winds on through Baghdad, Adrianople and ‘Akká, and through the wider story of suffering and imprisonment.
subjects.arc: Begin with companionship through displacement, establish the route and its costs, then explore the wider purpose discerned in the journeys.

order.why: Open with a companion remembered through exile, service, and final reunion with God.
shortened: Thou wert with thy Lord in times of hardship and tribulation until thou wert exiled with Him from the Land of Ta by reason of what the hands of the wicked had wrought. And thou didst arrive with thy Lord in Zawra, the place which the All-Merciful made the seat of His throne for successive years.

And thou didst migrate once again from Iraq with the Luminary of the horizons, and stood before His face morning and evening until thou didst arrive with thy Lord in the Land of Mystery which was named Adrianople, and from thence to the Most Great Prison.

And thou wert with Him for numbered years, and present before the Wronged One morning and evening, until thou didst soar on the wings of longing unto God, the Lord of the Day of the Covenant, and the verses of thy Most Glorious Lord drew thee to the Supreme Paradise - that station wherein naught can be seen save the manifestations of the grace of thy Lord, the All-Bountiful, the Ancient of Days.

order.why: Name the repeated loss of home.
shortened: Consider how He was driven from His native land with what tribulation and persecution - from Tehran to Iraq, from Iraq to the renowned city, thence to the land of Bulgaria, and thence to this Prison of tribulation. Four times was He rendered homeless.

order.why: Set out the sequence of destinations in a concise account.
Reaffirm the experience of being moved from country to country.
shortened: O servant of Baha! The Ancient Beauty and the Most Great Name (may my spirit be sacrificed for His loved ones) was repeatedly exiled, taken from land to land and country to country.

order.why: Read an earlier episode of official pressure and departure for Karbila.
Consider the account of the move from Istanbul to Edirne.
Connect banishment with imprisonment and dispossession.
Confront the severity assigned to the final place of confinement.
shortened: Again they banished Him to Constantinople, and from Constantinople a third time to Rumelia, and afterwards sent Him to the most desolate of the world's fortresses, the citadel of Akka, where they imprisoned Him. No worse place for exile and imprisonment could be imagined than this, nor could there be a more severe banishment than to be exiled four times and finally imprisoned in a fortress like Akka.

order.why: Hear the deprivation described on entering ‘Akká.
shortened: Then they turned with blackened faces against faces of light, and banished Us from the Land of Mystery and made Us enter 'Akka. It is the most desolate of the cities of the world. When We entered the prison, its doors were guarded by souls who had never inhaled the fragrance of faith from the Egypt of certitude, nor had the breezes of the All-Glorious ever wafted upon their hearts. Three successive months passed and We did not enter a bath. Thus did it befall the Youth at the hands of those who denied God's favor after its descent.

order.why: Introduce the summons to hear the Sultan’s decree.
Read the reported decree of perpetual imprisonment.
Consider the long duration of confinement recalled by the selection.
Notice the refusal to treat available dignity and ease as incompatible with endurance.
Read the figurative account of opposition and refuge.
shortened: After the Sun of Truth had set below the horizon of Iraq, the people of discord surrounded Him, bound Him in chains, and assailed Him with permissible spears and poisoned arrows. So He left the City of Peace and hastened to the shelter of the tents, and dwelt near the Most Great Prison in safety and peace.

order.why: See how remembrance of the exiles becomes consolation for others.
shortened: Though you have been persecuted, made homeless, and humiliated, this was in the path of that loving Friend, Who was Himself exiled from Iran to Iraq, from Iraq to the Great City (Constantinople), from thence to Rumelia (Adrianople), and from Rumelia to this afflictive prison.

order.why: Distinguish the grief of departure from the purpose later discerned.
Consider the writings and wider proclamation associated with banishment.
shortened: Later, when the Blessed Beauty was exiled, the friends were grief-stricken and disheartened while the enemies rejoiced, saying 'Praise be to God, Baha'u'llah was exiled.' But had the Blessed Beauty not been exiled, the Tablet to the King and the Tablet to Ra'is would not have been revealed and the Cause of God would not have been spread abroad.

order.why: Follow the text’s own invitation to compare Abraham’s migration.
shortened: It behoves us to ponder awhile that if the emigration of Abraham from Ur to Aleppo in Syria produced such results, what will be the effect of the exile of Baha'u'llah from Tihran to Baghdad, and from thence to Constantinople, to Rumelia, and to the Holy Land!

order.why: Read the chain of places through the reported interpretation of divine purpose.
shortened: What outward relation exists between Shiraz and Teheran, Bagdad and Constantinople, Adrianople and Acca and Haifa! God worked patiently step by step through these various cities according to his own definite, eternal plan – so that the prophecies and predictions as foretold by the prophets may become fulfilled.

order.why: Consider the departure and arrival as signs whose meaning calls for reflection.
Complete the linked readings with a reflection on effects difficult to grasp in the present.
shortened: Of a certainty, it is difficult to imagine its full effect at the present, but for those endowed with discernment and possessing absolute certitude, such conception poses no obstacle and [its realization] is manifest as the sun.

order.why: Revisit the route in another preserved formulation.
shortened: The Bab was likewise banished from Shiraz to the banks of the river Araxes, but auspicious indeed were the results of His banishment! The Blessed Beauty---may my soul be offered up for His loved ones---was exiled from Persia to Iraq, thence to Constantinople, and later to the Land of Mystery, before being transferred to the Most Great Prison.

order.why: Read the report contrasting forced removal with respect shown along the way.
shortened: During the time Baha'u'llah resided in Mesopotamia he displayed marvelous grandeur and power, notwithstanding the enmity and opposition of the Shah and the noblemen of Persia. Learned men of all nations sought him and were humble in his presence. They received from his holy tongue answers to their questions, and not a single soul left his blessed presence unsatisfied. When the ulama saw that Baha'u'llah exercised such influence in Bagdad they caused him to be exiled to Constantinople. However, he was sent, not as other exiles, but with honorable escort, and the officials en route, including the governor general, showed him great respect.

order.why: Read the fuller account of official attempts to extinguish the Cause.
shortened: They subjected Baha'u'llah, therefore, to severe hardships so that He would be forced to seek permission to leave Persia, and they imagined that the lamp of the Cause would be thereby extinguished. But this persecution produced the contrary effect: The Cause grew in stature and its flame waxed brighter. It had until then spread only within Persia; this caused it to spread to other regions.

Finally the Persians said, "None of these locations was a place of humiliation: He must be sent to a place where He will be disgraced and subjected to trials and persecutions, and where His kindred and followers will suffer the direst afflictions." Thus they chose the prison city of 'Akka, which was reserved for rebels, murderers, thieves, and highway robbers, and in this wise they made Him associate with such people.

questions: How does following a companion’s experience change the way we read a sequence of banishments?
What differences appear between the meaning of an event at the time and the meaning later discerned in it?
What does the comparison with Abraham illuminate, and how does a divine summons differ from forced expulsion by authorities?
How can a conviction of spiritual purpose coexist with clear recognition of injustice and loss?
What forms of practical companionship might these accounts inspire toward people facing displacement today?

neighbors.invitation: Read the experience of travel, family illness, and separation in greater detail.
Consider the recollection of hunger after the family’s possessions were plundered.
Explore a later vision of a place of confinement becoming a center of learning and service.

references.label: 1 · Genesis 12:1–4 (King James Version)
references.note: Abram is called to leave country and kindred, with a promise that blessing will extend to all the families of the earth. The compilation itself invites reflection on Abraham’s migration. Compare the relation between departure and a wider religious purpose while distinguishing the biblical summons from the coercive banishments described here.

subjects.displayTitle: The early years: generosity, insight, and a gathering purpose
subjects.introduction: The door of His house stood open, and people wondered at it: a young man from a family of ministers who wanted no rank, solved the hardest problems put to Him in learned gatherings, and gave to every poor person until the wise concluded that He must be pursuing a lofty cause not yet apparent. The early years of Bahá’u’lláh, are a study in how a purpose becomes visible before it is announced. A boy still short of maturity hears two turbaned scholars debate whether Gabriel outranks the Prophet’s servant and asks what fruit such discussion has ever borne. A youth without the insignia of learning explains a tradition the students had failed to interpret. Then come the Báb’s Cause, teaching night and day in Núr, suspicion, a hostile crowd, a ruined estate, and beside all this the memory of ten thousand poplars and tea prepared at dawn in a garden. Luke’s scene of the young Jesus among the teachers offers a comparison for how early insight is remembered [1]. The story continues into the Síyáh-Chál, the years in Baghdad and Sulaymáníyyih, and the long road of banishment.
subjects.arc: Begin with generosity and insight, move through the support of the Báb’s Cause and growing danger, and end with personal memories and the purpose of concord.

order.why: Open with generosity, detachment, and the unexpected direction of a young life.
shortened: All were amazed that a child of such intelligence, from a family of ministers, would have no desire whatsoever for rank and position, even though any position was possible for the Blessed Beauty. Despite this, He showed the utmost detachment and generosity, giving charity to every poor person and consoling every destitute one. The door of His blessed house was open, and this caused even more wonderment that without accepting any work or position He showed such generosity and munificence.
Some wise ones said that the Blessed Beauty had other thoughts and was pursuing a lofty cause not yet apparent - a day would come when this matter would become clear.

order.why: Hear the concise self-description of family background and outward learning.
Examine the question of what religious argument actually yields.
shortened: Among other things, she mentioned that we must know and understand who was higher - Gabriel or Qanbar, the servant of the Prince of Believers. Although this Wronged One had not yet reached physical maturity, He was greatly amazed at the understanding of those two heedless ones. In any case, that person, in his own imagination, counted such utterances among divine knowledge and supposed himself to have ascended to the highest station of mystical insight, unaware that he was recorded and numbered before God as among the worshippers of names. After pausing for a few minutes, this Wronged One stated that if Gabriel was the one referred to in the Mighty Book where it states "The Faithful Spirit hath descended with it upon thy heart," then Qanbar had no station in comparison.
What fruit or effect have they observed from such discussions, and what is gained from such mentions?

order.why: Read a second account of the encounter about spiritual rank.
shortened: Finally, their discourse culminated in one of them, who was the greater and more prominent, stating that we must know whether Gabriel is higher than Qanbar. When this Wronged One heard these words, His whole being was set aflame, yet We chose silence. After a few minutes it was mentioned: "O honored one, if Gabriel is he who is referred to in 'The Faithful Spirit brought it down upon thy heart', then at that station Master Qanbar was not even present." Now consider the heedlessness and unsuitable knowledge of the people. The station of Gabriel is the inner reality of the Messenger of God, yet he was arguing that Qanbar was more exalted because he was related to Ali.

order.why: Consider the reported interpretation offered by a youth without the outward insignia of learning.
Attend to the remembered circumstances of birth and early childhood.
Notice a recollection of personal devotional practice.
shortened: This Wronged One, in the land of Ta [Tehran], would fast on the eve of Ashura, and on the following day would partake of tea and bread after noon. This was the practice of the Wronged One, and some of the souls present are aware of this and know it.

order.why: Connect religious conduct with consideration for others in sacred places.
Pause over a place of gathering remembered for its beauty.
shortened: In the early days of the Cause, in the year '65, the Blessed Beauty chose that place because it was somewhat secluded. In summer there was a mountain like this Mount Carmel. At the foot of that mountain there was a garden with a stream of water - most delightful. There was an upper level with a garden and building. From there, one would descend thirty or forty steps to the second level, which also had a garden and grapevines.

order.why: Mark the turn toward spreading the Báb’s Cause.
Read the account of active teaching and the setting of a later imprisonment.
shortened: The second time, the Blessed Beauty was imprisoned in Amul, and it happened thus: After Badasht, He proceeded to Nur where He taught the Cause.

Day and night He taught, without a moment's rest. Many souls became believers. There were even four mujtahids there, two of whom were sons-in-law of the former mujtahid, Mirza Muhammad-Taqi, and the rest were his relatives. In one gathering, He taught all four mujtahids in such a way that afterward, all four rushed to kiss His blessed shoes.

order.why: Consider the effort to assist the defenders of Tabarsi.
Notice the visits of princes during imprisonment.
Read the encounter with official accusation and an offered position.
shortened: The Amir-Nizam asked Us one day to see him. He received Us cordially, and revealed the purpose for which he had summoned Us to his presence. 'I am well aware,' he gently insinuated, 'of the nature and influence of your activities, and am firmly convinced that were it not for the support and assistance which you have been extending to Mulla Husayn and his companions, neither he nor his band of inexperienced students would have been capable of resisting for seven months the forces of the imperial government.
We vehemently protested against such accusations, and refused to accept the position he hoped to offer Us. A few days after that interview, We left Tihran for Karbila.

order.why: Follow the return from pilgrimage into the hospitality of an acquaintance.
shortened: When Baha'u'llah returned from His pilgrimage to Karbala, the brother of the Grand Vizir Abbas Goli Khan according to the custom of the country invited him to stay with him the first few days of his arrival. Baha'u'llah accepted the invitation and took possession of the quarters which were prepared for him.

order.why: Consider the changing attitude of government toward material privilege.
Confront the seizure and destruction of the family property.
shortened: In like manner, the country house and mansion of Baha'u'llah in Mazindaran were seized and destroyed by the oppressors. Yet, His Mansion in the Kingdom was adorned and beautified and an everlasting edifice was raised up.

order.why: Complete the linked readings with the child’s recollection of sudden hunger.
shortened: In Tehran one night we had everything, the next morning all was plundered. It reached the point where we did not have sustenance to stay alive. I was hungry with no bread. My mother would pour some flour in my hand which I would eat in place of bread.

order.why: Return to the intimate memory of a garden and tea prepared at dawn.
shortened: Long before sunrise, I would open my eyes admiring with wonder this infinite universe of God. Then all at once the nightingales, in sweet melodies break into sweet concert of divine music, the gentle murmur of the rills flowing on all rides reached to the ears and the zephyr passing through the leaves making the noise of a soft sweeping handclap and applause. In the early morning the blessed Perfection would rise and prepare tea for all of us and while the sun was dawning from the Eastern horizon we were gathered around him, drinking tea and enjoying the heavenly scene all around us".

order.why: Read another remembered gathering place associated with the early Cause.
shortened: For there, in that pure and hallowed field, the Blessed Beauty---may my life be offered up for His loved ones---took up residence for an entire summer. There He resided in the garden of Haji-Baqir, which consisted of three terraces overlooking a lake. This was in the earliest days of the Cause, when that district became the throne of the Lord of the Kingdom. A large stone platform was raised in the heart of the lake, with a tent in the centre and gardens all around. About one hundred and fifty friends would gather, and at night hymns of praise would rise up to the Concourse on high. Those were wonderful times indeed. The Blessed Beauty would frequently make mention of that place.

order.why: Confront the reported danger of a hostile crowd.
Consider the account of threats and pressure to depart.
shortened: And an order had been sent to the governors of Mazindaran that they should seize Us and subject Us to punishment. But His Majesty the Shah departed this life; and thereafter Amir-Nizam, in the council of the notables, declared: "How greatly hath he harmed the state---and yet, in the utmost dignity, he dwelleth in Tihran!" It was a time fraught with danger, and most of the eminent urged me to depart toward some other quarter.

order.why: Distinguish the two journeys recalled in the supplied account.
shortened: The Blessed Beauty - may my spirit be a sacrifice for His loved ones - made two journeys to Baghdad and Karbala. One journey was after the martyrdom of the Bab - may my spirit be a sacrifice for Him - during the time of Mirza Taqi Khan, the Prime Minister Atabik, and one journey was after the attempt on the Shah's life when He was exiled and banished.

order.why: Close with the personal recollection of distress and the declared purpose of concord and unity.
shortened: But when the ocean of forgiveness and grace appeared, therefore in those days I beseeched God for that which was the cause of love, fellowship and unity among all who are on earth -- until, on the second of the month of the Birth before the Dawning, all my mental states, my words and thoughts, were turned upside down, an inversion that bore the glad-tidings of the Ascent.

After the Most High Pen [Qalam-i A'la=the Bab], We abrogated all that which was the cause of hardship and discomfort and strife by Our decisive decree, and We revealed and implemented all that which was a source of concord and unity.

questions: What connections emerge between the accounts of penetrating insight and those of generosity toward the poor?
How do the selections challenge the assumption that titles or outward signs of learning establish spiritual understanding?
What does comparing these recollections with Luke’s account of the young Jesus help us notice about religious biography?
How do memories of beauty and family life deepen the impact of the passages about dispossession?
What might it mean to ask of religious discussion, as these selections do, what fruit it produces in human life?

neighbors.invitation: Follow an account in which spiritual affection leads to friendship and material assistance.
Read the fuller account of the encounter with the Amir-Nizam.
Continue into the daily life of a community in exile.

references.label: 1 · Luke 2:46–52 (King James Version)
references.note: Luke portrays the young Jesus listening and asking questions among the teachers, whose response is astonishment at His understanding. The scene also includes His parents’ concern and a saying they do not understand. Compare how early insight and family experience are remembered in a religious life, without treating the two narratives as identical or flattening their distinct claims.

subjects.displayTitle: The commissions of inquiry: justice under pressure
subjects.introduction: The Commission of Investigation sent by the Sultan came to ‘Akká, went straight to the house of the accusers, asked the authors of the accusation whether it was true, and departed satisfied. Plaintiff, witness and judge had collapsed into one party, and an inquiry that treats the charge as the verdict can discover nothing. The charges themselves, a fortress on Mount Carmel, a banner waving over the tribes, a new sovereignty, were answered in a memorandum of such irony that He thanked the commissioners for attributing miracles to a lone prisoner. Beneath the irony runs something steadier: a refusal to meet the inspectors, calm while coded telegrams discussed exile or hanging, and the quiet dispatch of seventy believers to Egypt before He declined the ship that would have carried Him to safety. The Qur’án’s command to bear witness justly even against oneself and one’s kin names the discipline the commissioners lacked [1]. The road leads on into ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s own narrative of His life, the opposition and persecution He met, and the Covenant-breaking from which the accusations sprang.
subjects.arc: Begin with the failure of impartial inquiry, examine accusations and restrictions, then follow composure, care for others, and the accounts of changed circumstances.

order.why: Open with the striking collapse of plaintiff, witness, and judge into the same group.
shortened: To be brief, a Commission of Investigation was appointed by the Sultan, may the glory of his reign endure. The Commission journeyed hither and immediately upon arrival betook themselves to the house of one of the accusers. They then summoned the group who, working with my brother, had prepared the accusatory document and asked them whether it was true. The group explained the contents of the document, stated that everything they had reported therein was nothing but the truth, and added further accusations. Thus they functioned at one and the same time as plaintiffs, witnesses, and judge.

order.why: Set that concern within the account of an officially ordered investigation.
shortened: Last year a number of the unfaithful, both from within and from without, both known to us and strangers, took before the Sultan of Turkey slanderous charges against these homeless exiles, bringing against us grave accusations with no basis in fact. The Government, conformably with prudence, determined to look into these charges, and dispatched a Commission of Investigation to this city.

order.why: Introduce the appointment of a commission in its briefest form.
Read the recollection of repeated personal interrogation.
shortened: Recently, a Commission of Inquiry has arrived from Istanbul. Each day, I go to the government office and they interrogate Me.

order.why: Preserve the separate reported episode involving a requested interview with Bahá’u’lláh.
shortened: One day they came to me and asked me to arrange an interview for them with Baha'u'llah. I told them I could not promise them; because it is beyond my jurisdiction. Motosarraf continued his begging and importunity but Khorsheed Bay explained the truth, that because they are commanded by the authorities in Constantinople to investigate this matter they cannot quite well disobey the order.

order.why: Consider the later recollection of a commission’s composition and character.
Examine the allegations and the account of their acceptance without verification.
shortened: They have prepared a petition filled entirely with lies and calumnies, including that this servant raised the banner of "Ya Baha'u'l-Abha" in this land, proclaimed it in city and village, called people to gather under this banner, incited rebellion and revolt against the government, built a fortress on Mount Carmel, erected a great edifice in Haifa, formed alliances with foreign military leaders, offered gifts and favors, established a new sovereignty and religion, made the Holy Shrine a place of pilgrimage for various peoples with the purpose of dividing the manifest religion, and brought certain officials and others under the banner of the Cause.

Therefore, a group of officials came to investigate, and immediately upon arrival met with the Covenant-breakers and investigated their claims. The contents of the petition were explained and detailed by the Covenant-breaker and his associates, and the investigating committee accepted it without verification and departed.

order.why: Read another account of inquiry confined to the accusers.
shortened: Regarding events and occurrences, if you ask, it is the same as was written before - some of the unfair ones among the Covenant-breakers and officers made pure fabricated reports to His Majesty the Sultan. A committee composed of several officials was appointed to investigate. They went directly to the enemies, the helpers of the Covenant-breakers, and investigated from them, and whatever they heard they confirmed.

order.why: Revisit the significance attached to the commission’s first place of residence.
Consider a statement that one allegation was examined and found unfounded.
See how suspicion affected work on a sacred building.
Read the account linking disturbances with internal hostility.
shortened: The purpose is that you should inform His Honor Haji in detail about the situation - that all these recent disturbances concerning the Commission of Investigation and other matters up until now have stemmed entirely from Mirza Badi'u'llah, who continuously reported the activities of Mirza Muhammad-'Ali and is now showing the utmost enmity and hatred.

order.why: Attend to the experience of restriction and surveillance.
Notice how public crisis disrupted ordinary correspondence.
Consider the reported refusal to respond to a sequence of official inducements.
Examine composure under threats of death or further exile.
shortened: Yet 'Abdu'l-Baha paid them no heed whatsoever and would not even consent to meet them. However much they schemed and complained, saying "We have come on behalf of His Imperial Majesty; we never expected to encounter such indifference" - despite all their reproach and rebuke, no importance was given to them. Rather, complete calm and composure were maintained, as if nothing was happening and perfect peace prevailed, even while coded telegrams would arrive constantly from the Sultan's palace, whose contents made clear their determination to either send 'Abdu'l-Baha to Fezzan, hide him in the depths of the sea, or hang him.

order.why: Read the practical care for the friends and the decision about an offered departure.
shortened: I then asked them to consult on the situation, since the boat was ready to take Me. These honored personages sat and consulted. Unanimously, they concluded that this departure was the best way out and that I should accept it.
After they informed Me of their unanimous decision, I replied, "No, this would not be good for the Cause. I must do what exalts the Faith."

order.why: Pause at the return of a commission while the outcome remained unknown.
shortened: The commission has returned. There were several matters which they investigated here and prepared a report that they will present in the great city. We shall see what results it yields. However, certain strangers who had the utmost corrupt association with Mirza Muhammad Ali interfered greatly in affairs and made tremendous calumnies and accusations, though they were entirely baseless.

order.why: Preserve another moment of waiting for a decision.
Hear the recollection of fear for ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s survival.
Read one account of the interruption of the threatening proceedings.
Consider another recollection of the dispersal of those involved.
Attend to the spiritual interpretation given to their reversal.
shortened: In fact, even members of the Commission of Inquiry, who every hour ordered a more severe persecution and spread a fresh calumny and who had joined our enemies and adversaries at 'Akka with the aim of destroying and effacing us, were overtaken by the wrath of God while returning to Constantinople.

order.why: Complete the linked readings with the reported changes in political and personal fortunes.
Begin the additional selections with the constraints on local teaching.
Read a further report of hostility before the commission.
shortened: These honored persons [That is, the Covenant-breakers] have sent a report to the Commission of Inquiry, which has resulted in the Commission's head moving with a vengeance to eradicate the Cause of God.

order.why: Close with the ironic reply that exposes the disproportion of the allegations.
shortened: The reason for My gratitude and thanks to that honoured Commission is this: in their first complaint they made Me deserving of every praise, eulogy, and honour, and attributed to Me a mighty miracle. For how could it be possible for a lone, lowly, helpless captive and stranger to acquire such power as to break the influence of a mighty state and establish a new government?

Again, I thanked them for the second complaint, for it indicated My strength and power---nay, it was a great miracle. For I am a prisoner, and yet, in the very condition of imprisonment, I have been able to build a strong fortress wherein I might withstand great ships of war.

As to the third complaint: how strange! Was the Government, with all its spies---whose number is as the sands---asleep throughout these two years? Or did a heavenly angel blind their eyes, so that they were heedless and failed to see that manifest banner waving over the heads of the tribes?
As to the fourth complaint: I am prepared to sell all My properties for only one thousand liras.

questions: What distinguishes a genuine investigation from a procedure that merely confirms what its participants already wish to believe?
How does the Qur’án’s demand for justice even against personal or family interests illuminate the failures described here?
How do composure and practical care for others appear together during the crisis?
What differences should a reader attend to among immediate reports, later recollections, and spiritual interpretations of events?
What habits of listening and verification could help a community resist the power of an alarming but untested allegation?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the difference between collective inquiry and contentious debate.
Read about ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s service under conditions of confinement.
Consider composure amid turmoil alongside a wider vision of the Holy Land.

references.label: 1 · Qur’án 4:135 (parallel translations, Quranic Arabic Corpus)
references.note: The verse calls for justice and truthful witness even when testimony runs against oneself, parents, or relatives, and warns against partiality toward wealth or poverty. Compare that demanding standard with the accounts of accusation and inquiry in this compilation. The comparison concerns the moral discipline of judgment; it does not turn the historical reports into a complete account of legal procedure.

subjects.displayTitle: Haifa and the Holy Land: a horizon of learning and service
subjects.introduction: Standing on a bare, rocky hillside above a small Ottoman port, a prisoner and exile described a mountain ablaze with light from top to bottom, and on its slopes a hotel whose door was open to every people, a university teaching the higher sciences, a house of worship, and homes for the incurable, the poor and the orphaned. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saw the bay become a harbour sheltering the ships of all nations, Haifa and ‘Akká joined into one city under the shade of trees, kings walking bareheaded up terraced gardens with flowers on their shoulders, and he said plainly that he would not live to see it in the body. What makes the vision more than a pleasant picture is that its beauty is never separated from learning, hospitality and care for the vulnerable. Isaiah had sung of a wilderness blossoming like the rose and the splendour of Carmel given to it, together with strength for feeble hands and fearful hearts, a kindred language of hope rather than a timetable [1]. Read beside the restrictions, suspicions and commissions of inquiry under which these words were spoken, they ask how a place of confinement could be imagined as a centre of service to the world. The way leads on to Mount Carmel itself, to the Shrines and the meaning of pilgrimage, and to the wider question of prophecy and its fulfilment.
subjects.arc: Begin with access to learning and care, widen toward gardens, pilgrimage, and international encounter, then read the historical hopes beside the circumstances in which they were voiced.

order.why: Open with the promise of knowledge and educational opportunity for the poor.
shortened: Mount Carmel will be a Mountain of Knowledge, Peace, and Protection in the future----the vineyard of God. We will not live to see this in the body but will view it spiritually. Mount Carmel will someday be covered with great universities and colleges of learning. Then the poor will enjoy the highest advantages from the establishment here of free institutions of education.

order.why: Imagine worship, learning, hospitality, and care sharing one mountain.
Develop the vision of institutions serving vulnerable people.
shortened: Now, in addition to the myriad powerful lamps that will floodlight this mountain brightly, I can see Mashriqu'l-Adhkars, hospitals, schools, homes for the handicapped, orphanages, and all other humanitarian enterprises will be erected on Mount Carmel.

order.why: Connect the fields around the holy places with a wider pattern of service.
shortened: All these fields will become schools, hospitals, homes for the elderly, orphanages, and various hostels. Eventually the kings of the earth will come from Haifa, from the Most Exalted Spot, carrying urns of flowers on their heads to the Holy Shrine. Akka and Haifa will become one in the future. All of it will become gardens and palaces and buildings and a place of pilgrimage for all who dwell on earth.

order.why: Widen the scene to a harbor receiving people from many nations.
shortened: This great semi-circular arm of the Mediterranean will be transformed into the finest harbor wherein the ships of all the nations will seek shelter and refuge. The great vessels of all the people will come to this port, bringing on their decks thousands and thousands of men and women from every part of the globe.

order.why: Picture the link between cities as a shaded and cultivated landscape.
shortened: The area between Akka and Haifa will all become developed. It will all become gardens, orchards and buildings. There will be beautiful gardens. It will be such that one can walk from Haifa to Akka under the shade of trees. This sea will be filled with ships. Between Haifa and Akka ships will drop anchor.

order.why: Pause over the concise hope of connection and development.
shortened: 'Akka and Haifa will be connected, and all this land will be fertile and developed.

order.why: Read the fuller view of buildings, gardens, light, and a sheltered harbor.
shortened: Now, as I glance into the future, I see the greatest port in the world here. This semi-circular bay will be a large harbor for ships, so that the entering boats may be protected from the waves and winds of the storm. This harbor will be filled with ships of the nations. All of these regions will be decorated by buildings and lofty palaces. Many gardens and flower beds will be made. There will be electric lights and from here to Acca will be flooded with them.

order.why: Connect the scene of light with humility in pilgrimage.
Consider the reported plan of terraces, gardens, and a boulevard.
shortened: Ere long this mountain will be developed. Many fine buildings will be raised upon it. The Shrine of the Bab will be constructed in the best possible way and most majestically. It will be surrounded with many gardens, displaying multitudes of flowers. Nine terraces will be constructed from the bottom of the mountain to the Shrine of the Bab, and nine more will be above it to the summit of the mountain. A boulevard will connect the seafront to the foot of the mountain, and it too will have gardens filled with flowers.

order.why: Preserve another recollection of terraced gardens and charitable institutions.
Follow the transformation of rocky ground into gardens and a place of pilgrimage.
shortened: The rocky crags of this mountain shall be transformed into gardens of flowers and roses, and shall become a place of pilgrimage for all the peoples of the world.
The edifice of the Most Exalted Shrine shall be expanded.

order.why: Consider the image of rulers approaching with flowers.
shortened: In the future, on foot and holding bouquets of flowers above their heads and carrying wreaths, the monarchs of the earth will come on pilgrimage to the Sacred Shrines.

order.why: Read the fuller account of pilgrimage routes, rest, and prayer.
shortened: Ships carrying the flag of "Ya Baha'u'l-Abha!" will anchor at the port [of Haifa] and kings will disembark. On foot and bareheaded, and with humility and modesty, and in a state of supplication and entreaty, chanting divine verses and prayers, they will attain to a visit of the Shrine of the Exalted One [the Bab]. On the path to the Shrine of the Exalted One, there will be pools of water, gardens and places for rest and respite.
Afterwards, with bouquets of flowers over their shoulders, and while reciting divine verses and prayers, they will visit the Shrine of Baha'u'llah.

order.why: Explore the spiritual significance assigned to the mountain and its future.
shortened: Attaining unto this Mountain [Mount Carmel] was the ultimate desire of the Prophets, and it is the point of adoration of the Supreme Concourse. All the past Manifestations have given glad-tidings regarding this place and this Dispensation, and their highest aspiration was to witness such a Day and to behold and take part in such happenings. Here the tabernacle of the Most Great Peace will be hoisted and the foundation of the wondrous Divine Order will be established. All this land will be built and developed.

order.why: Attend to the invitation to perceive Haifa’s spiritual dimension.
Read the historical hope linking cultivation, commerce, and the gathering of a people.
shortened: All of these barren fields will become fertile and cultivated. The scattered tribes of the Jewish people will be united. This region will become the center of industry and commerce, and will be refined and populated. Of this there is no doubt.

order.why: Place that hope within the commentary’s interpretation of scriptural promise.
shortened: Likewise Israel, which had been scattered throughout the world, was not gathered together in the Holy Land in the course of the Christian Dispensation, but in the beginning of the Dispensation of Baha'u'llah this divine promise, which has been clearly stated in all the Books of the Prophets, has begun to materialize. Observe how from all corners of the world Jewish peoples are coming to the Holy Land, acquiring villages and lands to inhabit, and increasing day by day to such an extent that all Palestine is becoming their home.

order.why: Hear the invitation addressed to Jewish visitors in its historical setting.
Read the recorded political expectations beside the call for unity among religious communities.
shortened: 'Abdu'l-Baha: "Palestine, it is clear, will be for England, and Syria will remain in the hands of France.

"If the Muhammadans, Christians and Jews unite, there will be great progress. The Jews are unpopular now, but they will progress, and they will come here to reside. In the Books of the Prophets this promise has been given and in the Tablets of the Blessed Beauty for the Jews of Persia, He has written that the promises which have been given to you, 'that you will be gathered together', will be fulfilled.

order.why: Consider the restrictions that shaped local activity during the period.
shortened: "This is true; but I am not training thee for these parts; the field of thy labor is beyond these limited confines. As thou knowest it is very easy for us to teach and spread the Cause in this country but the government will rise immediately against us and the Blessed Tombs of Baha'u'llah and the Bab will be demolished by the hands of a fanatical mob. This is one of the many reasons that we must not raise our voice in Turkey."

order.why: Complete the linked readings with composure amid a threatening present.
shortened: As for the events at the Holy Spot, this land is in turmoil, and all are expecting that a great calamity will befall these wanderers, and suddenly some matter will occur and this land will be transformed. However, the tranquility, composure and dignity of Abdu'l-Baha keeps all calm, to such an extent that perhaps a newcomer might think nothing is happening. But the divine friends must never be affected by the occurrences in this land and must not await news and events from this land.

order.why: Return to the vision of light expressed through institutions of learning and care.
shortened: However, regarding the future of Carmel, I now behold the whole of this mountain basking in brilliant lights and the Haifa harbor as the anchor point of thousands of steam ships.
Likewise verily I see and behold the future effulgence of hospitals, schools and sanatoriums and the Mashriqu’l-Adhkar established on this mountain.

order.why: Connect urban development with sciences, arts, and international pilgrimage.
shortened: Houses for the infirm will be formed, hospitals will be established, universities will be built, schools will be founded, orphanages will be constructed, and lofty palaces and noble buildings will be raised around the Most Exalted Shrine.

Leaders and kings of various peoples will come in groups to visit the Holy Shrine and the Most Exalted Shrine. The lights of the shore will illuminate the dark nights into a unified radiance. Akka and Haifa will become a great center of magnificent enterprises and the dawning-place of the lights of sciences and arts.

order.why: Read Carmel’s rejoicing in the language of separation and reunion.
shortened: O Carmel! Thou didst taste the poison of separation through ages and centuries; now the honey of reunion hath come unto thee, inasmuch as the Countenance of the Ancient of Days hath turned toward thee from this direction which was recorded in the Mother Book by the Pen of the All-Merciful. The rapture of the utterance hath seized all created things.

order.why: Close with the hope of the land becoming a divine rose garden.
shortened: Read the Persian Bayan from beginning to end for the friends and explain its questions. God willing, a day will come when that region and land will become a divine rose garden and the Most Glorious Kingdom will encompass it. This is the desire of the sincere ones and this is the hope of the believers.

questions: What makes the envisioned beauty of the mountain inseparable from education, hospitality, and care?
How does Isaiah’s language of restoration deepen or complicate the way we read these visions of development?
What can the variety of reports and recollections teach us about reading a hoped-for future with both reverence and attention to context?
How does remembering confinement and suspicion change the meaning of a vision open to people from every land?
What could it mean for the design and use of any shared place to express a commitment to human well-being?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the suspicion surrounding construction on Mount Carmel.
Read the conditions of arrival in ‘Akká against the later horizon of service.
Explore the relationship between spiritual illumination and social development.

references.label: 1 · Isaiah 35:1–6 (Hebrew–English text, Mechon Mamre)
references.note: Isaiah joins the blossoming of wilderness and the splendor of Carmel with encouragement to the fearful and images of restored human capacities. Compare the interplay of landscape, hope, and human flourishing with these selections on gardens and institutions of service. The scriptural passage offers a language for comparison, rather than a timetable for the details in the historical reports.
